title: Links, Images, and Paths
description: Create links and images, distinguish relative from absolute paths, predict path resolution, diagnose broken links/images, and write effective alt text.

objectives.statement: Create links with the anchor element and images with the img element using meaningful attributes.
Distinguish relative paths from absolute URLs and predict how a relative path resolves from the current document's location.
Diagnose and correct a broken link or missing image caused by an incorrect path.
Decide whether an image is informative or decorative and write alt text accordingly.

content.title: Links, Images, and Paths
content.hook: A broken image icon or a link to nowhere is usually a path problem, not a typo in the tag itself.
content.context: This lesson connects HTML markup to the filesystem: where things actually live relative to each other.

content.title: Where Things Actually Live
content.text: The anchor element <a> creates a link using its href attribute; the img element embeds an image using its src attribute and describes it with alt. Both href and src can point somewhere in two different ways: an absolute URL fully specifies a location, protocol and domain included (like https://example.com/logo.png), while a relative path is resolved starting from the location of the current document — not from the site's root — unless it explicitly starts with a leading slash. If a page at /blog/post.html references an image with src="images/photo.jpg", the browser looks for that image inside a folder called images sitting next to post.html, not next to the site's root.

callout.text: Moving an HTML file to a different folder can silently break every relative path inside it, because the starting point for resolution just changed.

content.keyTakeaway: A relative path is always resolved relative to the current document's own location.

content.prompt: A file at `/site/pages/about.html` contains ``. Where will the browser look for that image?
options: It will search the entire site for a file named team.jpg
content.explanation: Because the path has no leading slash, it resolves starting from about.html's own folder, /site/pages/, not from the site root.

feedback.correct: Right — relative paths start from the current document's folder.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite — trace from where about.html itself lives, not from the site root.

content.title: Fix the Broken Image
content.prompt: This page's image isn't showing up. The HTML file lives at /site/pages/about.html, and the actual image file lives at /site/assets/team.jpg. Find and fix the path.
content.bugDescription: The relative path 'assets/team.jpg' resolves relative to /site/pages/, so the browser looks for /site/pages/assets/team.jpg — which doesn't exist. The real file is one level up, at /site/assets/team.jpg.
fixRequirements: The src should correctly point to /site/assets/team.jpg from about.html's location
hints: Where does 'assets/team.jpg' resolve to from /site/pages/, and where does the real file actually live?
You may need to go up one directory level first.

feedback.correct: Right — going up one level with ../ gets you from /site/pages/ to /site/, then into assets/.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the HTML file's folder to the image's real folder — you need to step up one level first.

content.question: A page includes a small decorative swirl graphic that adds no information — it's purely visual flair. What should its alt attribute be?
content.explanation: A purely decorative image should use an empty alt so screen readers skip it, rather than announcing a meaningless filename or description.

feedback.correct: Right — empty alt tells assistive technology there's nothing informative to announce.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite — for purely decorative images, an empty alt (not a missing one) is the correct choice.

content.title: What You Should Take Away
takeaways: Links use href; images use src and alt.
A relative path resolves from the current document's own location, not the site root.
Decorative images should use an empty alt; informative images need a real description.
